**Claim:** Yes, $g_n$ converges pointwise almost everywhere.

**Proof.**

Set $d_k := g_{k+1} - g_k \in L^2([0,1])$, so that $\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \|d_k\|_2 < \infty$. Define the pointwise partial sums
$$H_N(x) := \sum_{k=1}^{N} |d_k(x)|, \qquad H(x) := \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} |d_k(x)| = \lim_{N\to\infty} H_N(x) \in [0,\infty].$$

By Minkowski's inequality, for every $N$,
$$\|H_N\|_2 \le \sum_{k=1}^{N} \|d_k\|_2 \le \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \|d_k\|_2 =: M < \infty.$$

The sequence $H_N$ is nonnegative and pointwise nondecreasing (since we add $|d_k| \ge 0$), and it is bounded in $L^2$ by $M$. By the monotone convergence theorem (applied to $H_N^2$, which is also nondecreasing and has bounded integral $\|H_N\|_2^2 \le M^2$), $H_N^2 \uparrow H^2$ in $L^1$ and
$$\|H\|_2^2 = \int H^2 = \lim_{N} \int H_N^2 \le M^2.$$

Hence $H \in L^2([0,1])$, and in particular $H(x) < \infty$ for almost every $x \in [0,1]$.

Now fix any $x$ with $H(x) < \infty$. Then $\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} |d_k(x)| < \infty$, so the series $\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} d_k(x)$ converges absolutely, hence converges. Since
$$g_n(x) = g_1(x) + \sum_{k=1}^{n-1} d_k(x),$$
the limit $\lim_{n\to\infty} g_n(x) = g_1(x) + \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} d_k(x)$ exists.

Therefore $g_n(x)$ converges for every $x$ in the full-measure set $\{H < \infty\}$, i.e. $g_n$ converges pointwise almost everywhere. $\blacksquare$
